measures.what_it_does: Lifts Timberland Regional Library's regular property tax levy from about $0.22 to $0.35 per $1,000 of assessed value for 2027 and 2028; the 2028 amount becomes the base for later limits. TRL says about 96% of its budget comes from this levy, and that the money would restore open hours, staffing, collections and programs after 2026 budget cuts. The measure is decided by the combined vote of all five TRL counties.
measures.cost_line: From $0.228924 to $0.35 per $1,000 of assessed value, about $14 million more in 2027. Estimates for a Thurston home range from about $40 a year on a $334,000 home (explanatory statement) to $59 a year on the $457,400 median (TRL) and $69 a year on a $530,959 home (statement for).
measures.pro_summary: The statement for (TimberStrong Libraries Committee) says the levy has not risen in 25 years and has been eroded by rising costs, and that approval would restore hours and staffing and expand collections and programs: 'a long overdue cost-of-living raise.'
measures.con_summary: The statement against (Sean Swope, Citizens for Accountable TR Libraries) says property owners already face rising bills, and that the library should first show it has cut costs, sought grants and managed existing resources better. It says a no vote 'is not a vote against libraries or literacy.'

taxes.basis: A yes vote is a levy lid lift, which the taxes pole_b names explicitly: it raises TRL's regular levy rate by more than half, from about $0.22 (exactly $0.228924) to $0.35 per $1,000, adding about $14 million in 2027.

measures.sources_note: Local voters' pamphlet pages 24-25 (S1) and sample ballot (S2); Auditor's past-results list (S3); TRL levy page, Q&A and board news release (S4-S6); JOLT, Nisqually Valley News, Daily World and Chronicle coverage (S7-S11); PDC queries (S12-S13). The outcome of Olympia's Oct. 6 support resolution was not confirmed.

measures.what_it_does: Authorizes a two-year educational programs and operations (EP&O) levy for Yelm Community Schools, which has had no local levy for 2025 and 2026 after four failed attempts. It would keep the programs in place in 2025-26, such as current class sizes, AP and electives, athletics, activities, nurses, security and school resource officers,. The district says a limited amount would also let the board bring back some cut programs, and that if the levy fails the state would move it into financial oversight.
measures.cost_line: Up to $11,194,449 in 2027 and $12,278,072 in 2028, at an estimated $1.50 per $1,000 of assessed value. That is the lowest rate that qualifies for full state levy equalization; the legal maximum is $2.50. No Yelm EP&O levy is being collected now, so this adds a tax to current bills.
measures.pro_summary: The statement for (Yelm Kids First) says that after repeated levy failures the district has already cut staff, programs and athletics, and that the levy pays for teachers, counselors, nurses, safety staff and activities the state does not fully fund.
measures.con_summary: The statement against (Martin Miller and Frank Vance) says voters have said no four times and the levy restores none of the cuts. It says the district used one-time capital money for recurring costs, and that residents should press Olympia to meet its 'paramount duty' instead of taxing neighbors.

taxes.basis: No Yelm EP&O levy is being collected in 2025 or 2026. A yes vote brings back an excess levy of an estimated $1.50 per $1,000, about $11.2 million in 2027 and $12.3 million in 2028, so relative to current bills it is a new tax rather than a like-for-like renewal.

measures.sources_note: Local voters' pamphlet pages 26-27 (S1) and sample ballot (S2); Auditor's past-results list and 2025 SOS results (S3, S11); district levy FAQ (S4); Nisqually Valley News coverage 2025-2026 (S5-S10); PDC query (S12). parental-rights is not mapped: the sources describe staffing, programs and operations, not notification, records or opt-outs.

measures.what_it_does: Authorizes Lacey Fire District 3 to issue up to $98.3 million in general obligation bonds, repaid by property taxes over up to 20 years. The money would build a new station north of I-5 (Britton Pkwy), replace Station 32 on the Yelm Highway corridor, and build a regional live fire training facility and a logistics warehouse, plus property, other capital improvements and apparatus. The district cites more than 18,000 calls a year and only one of five stations north of I-5.
measures.cost_line: About $0.23 per $1,000 of assessed value, or about $9.60 a month on a $500,000 home, per the explanatory statement; the district's fact sheet gives $0.22 to $0.25 ($8 to $11 a month). Bond money cannot pay salaries or operations.
measures.pro_summary: The statement for (Steve Brooks and Tom Carroll) says calls are up 43% in ten years, a disaster could cut off the area north of I-5, and building now avoids higher construction costs later.
measures.con_summary: No statement against was filed; the pamphlet says no one in the jurisdiction contacted the Auditor to write one.

taxes.basis: A yes vote adds a new excess property tax of about $0.23 per $1,000 (about $9.60 a month on a $500,000 home) for up to 20 years to repay $98.3 million in capital bonds. It is a moderate new tax for capital projects, not an operating levy.

measures.sources_note: Local voters' pamphlet page 28 (S1; the page also carries a stray 'Fire Protection District 12' heading and ballot title left over from the November 2025 pamphlet, see S11) and sample ballot (S2); Auditor's past-results list (S3); district bond page and fact sheet (S4-S5); JOLT coverage (S6-S9); PDC query (S10). The outcome of Lacey's Oct. 6 support resolution was not confirmed, and the remaining term of the 2017 bond was not found.

measures.what_it_does: Authorizes the West Thurston Regional Fire Authority (Rochester and Littlerock) to collect a one-year excess maintenance and operations levy in 2027. The ballot title covers maintenance and operations to keep current fire and EMS service. The authority cites failing apparatus, a facility water system replacement and an aging fleet, and the statement for says all the money will go to apparatus replacement and facility maintenance. Earlier M&O levies failed in 2022 and 2024, and the August 2026 levies were short of 60% on election night.
measures.cost_line: $1,547,228 in 2027, about $0.36 per $1,000 of assessed value: at most $15 a month ($180 a year) on a $500,000 home. Needs 60% approval.
measures.pro_summary: The statement for (Tyler Mason and Cathe Linn) says many frontline vehicles are at or past their service life, and that stations need HVAC, roof, electrical and plumbing work. It says replacing equipment before it fails costs less than waiting for emergencies.
measures.con_summary: No statement against was filed; the pamphlet says no one in the jurisdiction contacted the Auditor to write one.

taxes.basis: A yes vote adds a one-year excess levy of about $0.36 per $1,000 on top of the regular fire levy. Recent M&O levies failed, so it adds to current bills, but it is small and lasts one year.

measures.sources_note: Local voters' pamphlet page 29 (S1) and sample ballot (S2); Auditor's past-results list and SOS 2022/2024 results (S3-S5); WTRFA Strategic Plan 2026-2030 (S6); Chronicle coverage of the August 2026 levies (S7-S8); PDC query (S9). Certified August 2026 results were not retrieved.
